en.title: Amazon OA #336: Return Records
en.description:
Implement the register, login and logout endpoints of a mock website. Process n requests in order and output the return value of each request.

register username password: if the username is not registered, create the user and return Registered Successfully (this does not log the user in); otherwise return Username already exists, leaving the existing password and login state unchanged.
login username password: if the user exists, the password matches and the user is not currently logged in, the login succeeds and returns Logged In Successfully; otherwise return Login Unsuccessful. A logged-in user who logs in again always fails, and the original session stays active.
logout username: if the user is currently logged in, log them out and return Logged Out Successfully; if the user does not exist or is not logged in, return Logout Unsuccessful.

Initially there are no users. Usernames and passwords are case-sensitive, users do not affect each other, and a failed request changes no state. The core API table was a missing image in the upstream snapshot; it was restored from the original image published on the source page.
en.input: The first line contains n. Each of the next n lines contains one request: register username password, login username password, or logout username, with fields separated by a single space. 1≤n≤100000; username and password are alphanumeric strings (0-9, a-z, A-Z) of length 1..10. Standard input is this site's adaptation of the string-array parameter.
en.output: Output n lines; line i is the return value of request i, which is one of Registered Successfully, Username already exists, Logged In Successfully, Login Unsuccessful, Logged Out Successfully, Logout Unsuccessful.
en.explanation: Original examples 1 and 2 keep their inputs. The fourth output of original example 2 was written as Login Unsuccessfully in the upstream text, which disagrees with Login Unsuccessful in the original table; this site uses Login Unsuccessful as in the table. David in its explanation refers to the input david. The third example is added by this site: registering twice does not overwrite the password, logging in again while logged in fails, and logout bob fails because of the different case.
hints: Each user only needs two pieces of state: the password and whether they are logged in.
A failed request must not change any state.
A user who is already logged in fails to log in again, whether or not the password is correct.
